title: Parity, Carry and Hedging
intro: Three relationships tie exchange rates to interest rates and prices: covered interest parity (which holds, by arbitrage), uncovered interest parity (which often fails, and that failure is the carry trade), and purchasing power parity (which works slowly, over years). This page derives each, shows how carry trades make and lose money, and explains how investors hedge currency risk.

blocks.text: Covered interest parity: the forward rate

Suppose USD rates are $i_{\$}$ and euro rates $i_{€}$ for one year, and EUR/USD spot is $S$ (dollars per euro). You can turn \$1 into a sure amount of dollars in a year two ways: invest at $i_{\$}$; or convert to $1/S$ euros, invest at $i_{€}$, and lock in the conversion back with a forward rate $F$ agreed today. With no risk in either path, they must pay the same, or traders would arbitrage the difference:

blocks.caption: Covered interest parity, for EUR/USD quoted as dollars per euro.

blocks.text: So the forward rate is not a forecast: it is spot adjusted for the interest gap. The higher-yielding currency trades at a forward discount (it buys less in the forward market), exactly enough to offset its extra interest. With $S = 1.08$, $i_{\$} = 4.5\%$ and $i_{€} = 2.5\%$, $F = 1.08 \times 1.045/1.025 \approx 1.1011$. The difference $F - S$ in pips is the forward points. Covered parity held almost exactly before 2008; since then small, persistent deviations (the cross-currency basis) have appeared because banks face balance-sheet costs, but they are small next to the rate gap.

This is also what currency hedging costs or earns: a US investor holding euro assets who sells euros forward locks in roughly the interest difference, here about 2% a year in their favor. A euro investor hedging US assets back to euros pays about the same 2%.
Uncovered interest parity, and why it fails
If investors didn't care about risk, the expected future spot rate would equal the forward rate, so the higher-yielding currency would be expected to fall by just enough to cancel its extra interest:

blocks.tex: E[S_{t+1}] \approx S_t \cdot \frac{1 + i_{\$}}{1 + i_{€}} \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad E[\%\Delta S] \approx i_{\$} - i_{€}

blocks.text: This uncovered interest parity (UIP) fails in the data. Eugene Fama (1984) and many later studies found that high-interest currencies, on average over short horizons, do not fall as much as UIP predicts, and often rise: the forward premium puzzle. Over long horizons and in crises UIP holds better, because that is when high-yielders collapse. The gap is the source of the carry trade's average profit and its occasional disasters.
The carry trade

A carry trade borrows a low-interest funding currency (classically the yen or Swiss franc) and invests in a high-interest target currency (the Australian or New Zealand dollar, the Mexican peso, the Brazilian real, the US dollar when its rates were high). The trader earns the interest difference, the carry, as long as the target currency doesn't fall by more than that difference. With leverage the interest gain is multiplied, and so is the currency risk:

blocks.tex: R_{equity} - i_f \approx L\,\big[(1 + i_t)(1 + \Delta s) - 1 - i_f\big]
blocks.caption: Return over the funding rate on the trader's own money, with leverage L, funding rate i_f, target rate i_t and change in the target currency Δs.

blocks.text: The break-even is a fall of about the rate gap (4% at the default settings). Carry has historically earned a positive average return with a Sharpe ratio comparable to stocks, but its returns are negatively skewed: years of small steady gains interrupted by sudden large losses when markets panic and funding currencies spike (1998, when the yen rose sharply against the dollar in days; 2008; August 2024). It is often described as 'picking up nickels in front of a steamroller'. Brunnermeier, Nagel and Pedersen (2008) showed that carry crashes coincide with funding stress and rising volatility, which is why the premium exists: carry loses exactly when investors can least afford it.
Purchasing power parity

Absolute PPP says a basket of goods should cost the same everywhere once converted: $S = P_{home}/P_{foreign}$. The Economist's Big Mac index is the playful version: if a Big Mac costs \$5.70 in the US and ¥480 in Japan, the PPP rate is about 84 yen per dollar; if the market rate is 150, the yen is 'undervalued' by about 44% on this measure. Real goods are not perfectly tradable (rent, haircuts, taxes, transport), so absolute PPP holds loosely at best.
Relative PPP is more useful: currencies of high-inflation countries tend to depreciate by about the inflation gap over time:

Deviations from PPP are large and die out slowly; studies typically find a half-life of three to five years (Rogoff's 1996 'PPP puzzle'). So PPP is a guide to long-run value, not to next year. The real exchange rate $S \cdot P_{foreign}/P_{home}$ measures how expensive one country is against another; the real effective exchange rate (REER) does it against a trade-weighted basket.
The international Fisher effect

Combine the Fisher equation (nominal rate ≈ real rate + inflation) with relative PPP and, if real rates are equal across countries, interest differentials should equal expected inflation differentials, and hence expected currency changes: UIP again. In the long run this is roughly right (high-inflation, high-rate currencies like the Turkish lira lose value steadily); in the short run carry wins on average.
Hedging currency risk

items: Forwards: sell the foreign currency forward for the amount you hold, rolling every month or quarter. Hedged share classes of funds do this for you.
Cost or gain: about the short-rate gap (covered interest parity), plus small trading costs. Hedging a low-rate currency back to a high-rate home currency earns carry; the reverse costs it.
Bonds: currency swings are usually larger than a high-grade bond's own volatility, so international bond funds are commonly hedged; unhedged foreign bonds are mostly a currency bet.

Stocks: many long-term investors leave foreign stocks unhedged, because currency moves partly wash out over decades and because a foreign currency often rises when home markets are in trouble, which adds diversification (strongly so for holders whose home currency is risk-sensitive). Hedging half is a common compromise to limit regret.
Natural hedges: companies with foreign revenue and foreign costs; investors who will spend in a foreign currency later.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Forward rate
blocks.text: USD/JPY spot is 150.00. One-year dollar rates are 4.5% and yen rates 0.5%. What is the one-year forward, and what does a yen-based investor earn or pay to hedge dollar assets?
solution: For USD/JPY (yen per dollar), $F = S \times (1 + i_{¥})/(1 + i_{\$}) = 150 \times 1.005/1.045 \approx 144.26$.

The investor hedges by selling dollars forward at 144.26 instead of 150: a cost of about $1 - 144.26/150 \approx 3.8\%$ a year, roughly the rate gap. This is why Japanese investors' hedged US bonds can yield less than JGBs when the rate gap is wide.
blocks.answer: about 144.3; a cost of about 3.8% a year

blocks.title: Carry break-even
blocks.text: You borrow francs at 0.5% and hold Mexican pesos at 10%. How far can the peso fall against the franc in a year before the unlevered trade loses money? With 5× leverage, what happens if the peso falls 12%?
solution: At a 12% fall: asset return $= 1.10 \times 0.88 - 1 = -3.2\%$. Over funding, levered: $5 \times (-3.2\% - 0.5\%) = -18.5\%$ of your own money.

blocks.title: Big Mac PPP
blocks.text: A Big Mac costs \$5.70 in the US and £4.50 in the UK. The market rate is GBP/USD 1.27. What does burger PPP say the rate should be, and is the pound over- or undervalued on this measure?
solution: PPP rate $= 5.70/4.50 \approx 1.267$ dollars per pound. The market rate of 1.27 is almost exactly at PPP; the pound is fairly valued on this measure.
